The levator palpebrae superioris muscle is innervated by the occulomotor nerve (III). This muscle elevates the upper eyelid and therefore loss of innervation to this muscle would cause the eyelid to droop (ptosis). However, this is not a sign of Horner's syndrome as it is a common condition and not one specific to Horner's syndrome. The superior rectus muscle is innervated by the occulomotor nerve (III). This muscle abducts the eye and therefore loss of innervation to this muscle would cause the eye to deviate laterally. The orbicularis oculi muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII). This muscle is responsible for closing the eyelids and therefore loss of innervation to this muscle would cause the eyes to remain open. The superior tarsal muscle is innervated by sympathetic nerves. This muscle elevates the upper eyelid and therefore loss of sympathetic innervation to this muscle would cause the upper eyelid to droop (ptosis). This is a sign specific to Horner's syndrome as it is not a common condition.

Angiotensin I and II is a part of the Renin-Angiotensin-System (RAS) in the kidneys. Angiotensin I is converted to Angiotensin II by ACE (Angiotensin Converting Enzyme). Angiotensin II is a potent vasocontractor and it also stimulates the release of aldosterone. Aldosterone causes reabsorption of sodium and water in the kidney, which increases blood volume and blood pressure. Angiotensin II is also responsible for increasing the release of renin from the juxtaglomerular cells in the kidneys. So ACE-I block the production of Angiotensin II, which leads to a reduction in blood pressure.

Local anaesthetic drugs block voltage gated Na+ channels in neurons, preventing propagation of action potentials. Parasympathetic neurons release Ach into the synaptic cleft which causes constriction of the pupil via contraction of the sphincter pupillae muscle. The release of Ach causes an action potential which propagates down the motor neurone to cause contraction. If the local anaesthetic blocks the voltage gated Na+ channels in this motor neurone, the action potential cannot propagate and therefore the pupil does not constrict. This is known as the corneal reflex.  The ciliary muscle can dilate the pupil via the sympathetic nervous system. Here the release of NA into the synaptic cleft causes an action potential which propagates down the motor neurone to cause dilation. If the local anaesthetic blocks the voltage gated Na+ channels in this motor neurone, the action potential cannot propagate and therefore the pupil does not dilate.  Therefore the overall effect of local anaesthetic drugs is a decrease in the corneal reflex.
